item.title: How to Live With a Partner Who Blames You for Everything
item.description:
Forgiveness

How to Live With a Partner Who Blames You for Everything

Survival techniques for living with a blame-shifter.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Some individuals routinely blame others rather than taking responsibility for their choices and behaviors.
  • People who get unjustly blamed by their partners often increase conflict when they try to correct them.
  • Redirection will produce better results than trying to correct a partner that habitually shifts blame.

Mentally healthy individuals accept that human beings err. They accept responsibility for their behavior and choices, and they don’t blame others. Some individuals are too fragile mentally to take responsibility for unwanted outcomes that result from their choices and behaviors. It makes them feel too broken and too vulnerable. Instead, they blame others, especially those closest to them. Healthy people don’t like to be falsely blamed and tend to argue with their blame-shifting partners. This seldom results in a satisfactory conclusion. It usually results in extended conflict. Use of redirection is likely to produce much better outcomes.

It is very natural to try to correct others when you are falsely accused. Healthy individuals can be circumspect and accept your point of view. Individuals who routinely shift blame onto others feel attacked when you try to correct them. They become defensive and escalate the conflict. The following is a typical example.

PJ was preparing Ali’s favorite dinner. While PJ was cooking an old friend called. They were on the phone for an hour and PJ lost track of time. When Ali got home they had the following conversation.

Ali: I am starving. I was looking forward to your wonderful dinner all day.

PJ: Well, you better turn around and get some takeout for dinner.

Ali: I thought you were going to cook my favorite meal tonight.

PJ: You couldn’t be happy with a baked chicken or a steak. You have to have a quiche.

Ali: I didn’t ask you to make me dinner, you wanted to. What happened?

PJ: I did make it but it burned. I tried to make your stupid complicated dish and you were late and it burned.

Ali: I was only five minutes late. It must have burned at least half an hour ago.

PJ: How do you know? You weren’t here.

Ali: The oven is cold.

PJ: You are ungrateful. I will never cook for you again.

Don’t Argue Over Blame

While Ali understandably does not like to be wrongly accused, there are no material consequences associated with assigning blame. The dinner burned, for whatever reason, and PJ and Ali have to make alternative plans for the meal. Ali would do best to not argue about blame and proceed directly to the solution.

Redirection

Ali will do best to redirect PJ from establishing blame to finding a solution for dinner and for PJ’s wish to make quiche for Ali. Once PJ revealed that the dinner was burned, Ali should have responded something like this:

Ali: That’s OK. How about we go out to dinner tonight and you can make quiche tomorrow night if you would like.

PJ: You are not angry that I burned the food?

Ali: It was an accident, right?

PJ: Of course.

Ali: I will help you clean up the oven when we get back from dinner.

Do Not Polarize

Source: Image by John Hain from Pixabay

PJ’s effort to avoid blame was to make it Ali’s fault. This is an effort to make Ali the bad one while PJ is free of responsibility. This search for a winner and a loser in this situation is competitive and hence divisive. PJ expects Ali to agree to a narrative where Ali is flawed and PJ is superior. The actual result is that Ali will be angry PJ for making false accusations and experience resentment.

If Ali is successful in redirection, competitiveness will be replaced by cooperation as they strive for a mutually beneficial solution. Resentment will be replaced by intimacy as they replace conflict with mutual support of a common goal.

The burden of redirection will probably almost always fall on Ali. The type of changes PJ needs to be able to tolerate errors comfortably will take tremendous effort and considerable time. Redirection may not always be successful. Presumably the benefits of sustaining the relationship with PJ will outweigh this burden for Ali.

If you are someone who finds it intolerable, or excessively painful, to take responsibility for errors in your life, it would behoove you to seek relief. Doing so through blame-shifting will disrupt your relationships. Lasting relief will require you to address the factors underlying your fragility. Psychotherapy can be very helpful in understanding the underlying fear of being flawed and associated feelings of vulnerability. This will help you to increase your sense of self-worth and confidence so that you can comfortably tolerate making the kind of errors that all humans do.

item.title: Dolly: The Powerful Female Archetype America Is Grieving
item.description:
Identity

Dolly: The Powerful Female Archetype America Is Grieving

Dolly Parton was contradictory, complex, and entirely herself.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • America is not just mourning a beloved musician but the loss of a rare, fully realized female archetype.
  • Modern celebrity significantly flattens the psychological depth of its female stars.
  • True human strength lies in internal complexity, not just external status.

Why are we grieving Dolly so deeply? Perhaps because she represented something we rarely see anymore: a woman allowed to be contradictory, complicated, powerful, and entirely herself.

Modern Celebrity and the Flattening of Female Archetypes

The sudden passing of Dolly Parton has caused America to fall to its knees. She was an iconic cultural titan who embodied beauty, power, wit, wisdom, and the relentless ability to be unapologetically herself in a world that constantly demands women compromise their edges. Modern celebrity significantly flattens the psychological depth of its female stars, forcing them over time to morph into smaller, meeker, more apologetic versions of themselves for fear of public ridicule and dwindling social media numbers. As a result, we are starved of complex female archetypes who embody a nuanced psychological blend of vices and virtues, light and darkness.

Andy Warhol famously observed the toxic nature of overexposure, noting how mass media and public obsession inevitably cannibalize a star's true identity—a phenomenon that famously reduced Marilyn Monroe from a complex human being into a flattened, tragic caricature. For this reason, contemporary female stars frequently find themselves pandering to the masses, hiding their moral ambiguities, internal calculations, and emotional conflicts behind a sanitized, highly curated veneer.

But this performative perfection misses a vital psychological truth: True human strength lies in internal complexity, not just external status. In reality, no person is completely good or bad. Humans are a complicated blend of flaws and virtues, and this inherent duality makes people real, interesting, and deeply resonant.

The psychologist Heinz Kohut wrote that humans require three specific relationships in life to develop a cohesive self: idolization, mirroring, and twinship. Idolization represents the gods, celebrities, and icons we look up to and idealize. Mirroring represents those who look up to us with adoring eyes, confirming our sense of worth. Twinship presents resonance—the deep feeling of connection with someone who shares our nature, vulnerabilities, and lived experiences.

Consider the cinematic experience of "Joker" (2019). Audiences experienced a profound, soulful resonance with the main character portrayed by Joaquin Phoenix. It was deeply disturbing precisely because he was warm, vulnerable, and relatable, yet simultaneously a villain. This duality created a perfect element of twinship; we saw our own capacity for darkness and isolation reflected back at us. Conversely, the traditional, seemingly perfect depiction of Superman—all virtue with no vice (save for a superficial vulnerability to Kryptonite)—fails to compete for this type of psychological connection. No one cries for a flawless Superman. No one ponders his internal world weeks later, because a character devoid of human flaws is hollow, one-dimensional, and fundamentally unengaging.

We encounter this exact psychological failure in many of today’s stars, who scrub away their rough edges to remain palatable. Dolly, however, was one of our last beacons of hope. She was a walking paradox—a radical feminist who looked like a hyper-feminine Barbie, an astute business mogul who acted with the disarming warmth of a country neighbor, and a fiercely private woman who lived under a global microscope.

How Dolly Parton Embodied Psychological Twinship and Complexity

Dolly masterfully balanced the pillars of Kohut's psychology. While her larger-than-life aesthetic invited global idolization, her razor-sharp wit and absolute transparency about her own artificiality (exemplified by her legendary quip, "It takes a lot of money to look this cheap") provided a profound sense of twinship. She was a flawless strategist who wore her self-constructed flaws on her rhinestone sleeve. She allowed us to see the calculation behind the charm, the grit behind the glamour, and the deep emotional resilience required to protect her empire. She was many things, but she could never be accused of being a hollow, one-dimensional figure stripped of the essential element of twinship. In losing Dolly, America is not just mourning a beloved musician; we are grieving the loss of a rare, fully realized female archetype—one who proved that a woman can be complicated, calculated, contradictory, and entirely whole.

item.title: Do Animals Experience Flow?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Do Animals Experience Flow?

Rethinking flow, consciousness, and the inner lives of animals.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • Flow emerges when challenge and skill are balanced, producing deep focus and absorption.
  • Animals demonstrate persistence, problem-solving, play, cooperation, and intrinsic motivation.
  • Human-centered inquiry methods may underestimate the complexity of nonhuman animal experience.
Do Animals Experience Flow?
Source: Leigh W. Jerome Ph.D.

In 2005, Nakamura and Csikszentmihalyi interviewed rock climbers, chess players, athletes, and artists, investigating why people choose to perform demanding, time-consuming tasks that offer no extrinsic rewards. We now know that people actively seek out experiences that induce flow. Flow is the intensely satisfying state that comes of becoming fully engrossed, energized, and focused on a challenging activity requiring high motivation and increased concentration (Csikszentmihályi, 1975). It is the complete absorption that can come on when the demands of an engaging activity are slightly beyond one’s current skill level. If the activity is too difficult, it produces anxiety, and if too slight, it can elicit boredom. But when there is a balanced dynamic between skill and challenge, an optimal flow experience emerges where attention narrows, time distorts, and distractions fade away. People who experience flow frequently report more joy and greater life satisfaction (Isham & Jackson, 2022).

It is interesting to note that flow has been advanced as being distinct from immersion. For example, watching a gripping movie or reading a riveting novel has been described as leading to genuine absorption but not flow, because the challenge-skill feedback loop is absent. However, there is considerable overlap between the concepts of immersion, flow, and presence (i.e., the sense of “being there”), and empirically, the distinctness has not been fully demonstrated (Michailidis, Balaguer-Ballester, & He, 2018). Further, while some physiological measures have been explored, the findings have been inconsistent. Flow remains primarily measured by self-report inventories, which are inherently filtered through perception and are thus vulnerable to bias. This muddiness brings to mind a new question: Do animals experience flow?

Historical Perspectives on Animal Consciousness

Consciousness has long been believed to be a uniquely human construct. Animals, lacking consciousness, have been presumed unable to experience subjective thoughts and emotions such as joy, pain, or compassion. These convictions, coupled with the fact that animals cannot verbally report their inner lives, have been judged as evidence that animals are able to become engaged and immersed in activities but lack the self-awareness required to experience flow.

Things have changed. There is now broad scientific consensus that birds and mammals do have conscious experience, and the realistic possibility that all vertebrates have some form of consciousness, including curiosity and information-seeking for its own sake. These insights have recently led to research in the nonhuman experience of immersion and flow. Nascent investigations are exploring how animals respond to challenge, progress in complex tasks, and winning and losing, and have suggested using behavioral measurements to look at these issues, including resistance to distraction, problem solving, and patterns of reward, engagement, and frustration (Humphreys et al., 2026).

To date, flow has not been empirically demonstrated in nonhuman animals; however, the problem may be the use of human-centered tests. Comparative cognition has a long history of discovering that capacities assumed to be uniquely human appear elsewhere, once researchers ask questions in ways that fit the animal being studied. Animals have been shown to have deep task-positive engagement during hunting, play, tool use, and foraging. Some animals demonstrate persistence beyond extrinsic reward-chasing, episodic-like memories, the ability to solve complicated puzzles, and enjoyment when playing games. Research also confirms that animals process varied emotions that drive their participation in their environments, such as stress, care, grief, fear, joy, and disgust. Historically, science has diminished animal capacity, particularly regarding consciousness, emotion, and pain. Perhaps we have yet to become sophisticated enough to recognize how nonhuman animals experience flow or develop tools that are sensitive enough to measure it.

Evidence of Complex Cognition and Intrinsic Motivation in Animals

There are so many ways of knowing. Different species have evolved varied perceptual systems, motivations, and ways of extracting information from the world around them. A lack of specialized instruments does not negate a reality; it simply means that modern science has yet to build a tool able to quantify it. We can find evidence that animals possess rich inner lives and hidden intelligence that standard human tests fail to measure. For example, intrinsic motivation in animals can be noted when they choose to work for a reward even when identical rewards are simultaneously available for free. Some animals use regional vocalizations and have distinct descriptive labels for specific predators. Migrating birds and sea turtles navigate thousands of miles using quantum radical-pair mechanisms, magnetic fields, and star maps to process sensory data. Further, while animals often choose a challenging route individually, there is evidence that some choose a difficult shared task over an easier, independent route.

There is a strong literature documenting cooperative-task studies between animals. Dogs, paired with other dogs or a human, actively track their partner’s behavior and adjust their own timing to it. Rooks can solve a rope-pulling task that requires simultaneous action from both birds. Chimpanzees, given a choice, recruit a partner only when the task requires one, and pick whichever of two candidates performs better on the task the day before. Dolphins use whistles to actively negotiate timing with a partner. In solitary animal-flow research, the challenge-skill feedback loop is necessarily internal. In a cooperative task, that loop instead runs between the two animals. This phenomenon has been documented in human group or team flow experiments in which groups share an “in the zone” state of peak collective focus, performance, and neural synchrony. People seek out team flow experiences because it blends high performance, deep social connection, and profound personal satisfaction into a shared group experience.

Nonhuman animals also show clear signs of enjoying collaborative problem-solving. They respond enthusiastically to engagement with others without urging, display playful interactions, and exhibit excited vocalizations during re-engagement. A 2025 international animal-welfare science consensus argues that an animal's good life cannot be defined merely by the absence of pain, hunger, and fear. Flourishing must in part include rewarding experiences, choice, agency, competence, and opportunities to pursue goals and achieve desired outcomes. If this is so, then the question of animals experiencing flow is more than a fringe question in animal science; it’s one we owe them an answer to.

item.title: How a Dog Named Freddie Taught His Human to Be Human
item.description:
Relationships

How a Dog Named Freddie Taught His Human to Be Human

Anna Heyward writes about her special relationship from Freddie's point of view.

Posted September 8, 2026

Key points
  • There are many dimensions to dog-human relationships, and Anna Heyward covers many of them in a new book.
  • A big theme of the book is seeing things from a point of view that’s not your own.
  • Imagining the life of another animal can end up making you more human, not less.
Source: Courtesy of Anna Heyward

Books about dog-human relationships are a dime a dozen, and it's not surprising that they vary greatly in quality for any number of reasons. However, when I started reading Anna Heyward's beautifully written new book, Living with Freddie: How a Dog Taught Me to Be Human, I knew I was in for a special treat.

In her outstanding book, Heyward writes about her special relationship with Freddie, and the trials and tribulations of separation anxiety, from his point of view. She craftily places the science and history of our relationship with dogs within a deeply personal story about the joy and the pain of living with, and trying to relate to, a nonhuman animal; a stunning meditation on the bond between beasts and humans.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Living with Freddie?

Anna Heyward: When I was in my twenties, I went out and got a dog without really knowing what I was doing. I thought it would be a fun addition to my life, and I thought I was grown-up enough to handle something as simple as having a dog. But there was nothing easy or simple about Freddie. He had some severe behavior problems that I had never heard of, thought about, or anticipated. I was living an exciting life in New York City working in art and magazine publishing, and I had never spent much time at all thinking about nonhuman animal life or consciousness. I thought of myself as a person who “loved animals,” but really I knew nothing. Then Freddie came along and presented me with this endlessly interesting, confronting, moving, complex, maddening problem. I started doing everything I could to meet the challenge of living with him, but I was swimming against the tide. What happened next changed the course of my life and career. I ended up becoming an animal trainer and going to graduate school to study animal behavior and welfare science.

I wrote this book, in part, because I was shocked by my own lack of knowledge, and the lack of knowledge of the general public, about animal behavior, including the behavior of the animals we live with. I also wanted to share the momentous, transformative experience of living with Freddie.

MB: Who do you hope to reach and why?

AH: The book has two intertwined threads—half from the diary I kept during the time I lived with Freddie, and half from the science and research I did after Freddie’s arrival. There’s the naive voice of me looking at this dog who turned my world upside down, and then the more informational voice that places the story into a larger picture.

Source: Random House/with permission.

The struggle that took place between me and Freddie, or, maybe, between Freddie and the world, is not unique. It will be very familiar to some readers. Especially to those readers who have ever had a dog, or an animal, disrupt their human relationships. As I learned in the years following Freddie’s arrival, what happened was the result of the uneasy symbiosis between dogs and humans. The relationship between dogs and humans is vaunted and cherished. We think it’s so wholesome, but I discovered that there are a lot of different dimensions to it. Some of them left me reeling, and some of them were painful to learn about,

When the creature you’re cohabitating with does not behave how you’d like or need them to behave, whether it’s a dog, a person, or some other animal, what do you do? I hope readers will recognize the experiences I have described of living with other animals, whether human or nonhuman, because part of the story is a human one, too. And also that they’ll see their own experiences with a different perspective.

If you’ve ever watched your dog sniff along the ground and noticed that some things seem to hold their attention and some things don’t, or if you’ve noticed that your dog seems unable to hear or pay attention to you in certain situations while at other times they do so willingly, you’ll be able to relate to the germ of this book. Trying to answer what seemed like simple questions like that ended up changing my views of human life in unexpected ways.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

AH: A big theme of the book is seeing things from a point of view that’s not your own. Or, at least, trying to. Human-animal relationships are more complex than we tend to think. There’s a lot of potential for suffering on both sides. Loving a dog does not automatically mean we understand what the dog is experiencing. Behavior that humans label “difficult” may reflect fear, stress, pain or unmet needs. I had to interrogate some of the moralizing views I didn’t realize I held. Freddie changed the way I think about love, responsibility, cohabitation, pain, and happiness.

MB: How does your book differ from others that are concerned with some of the same topics?

AH: It was important for me to avoid some of the clichés and received ideas that I found in other books in the genre. Also, I did not want this to be the kind of book in which the animal is simply a symbol or a device to look at the human. There’s nothing wrong with doing that, and there are some books in that mold that I love, but I wanted the writing in this book to be based on Freddie’s experience. Or at least, as close to it as I could get. While we can’t escape our own experiences, there are tools we have at our disposal to relate to the experiences of other beings.

MB: Are you hopeful that, as people learn more about what it really means to live with and love a dog, they will give their companion canine a better and more fulfilled life?

AH: I wouldn’t say the book tells a “happy” story, but it does have a sort of happy ending. Or at least, a mixed ending. And while a lot of the experience was quite painful, and the learning curves were steep, that is what I hope readers will see in the book—I don’t believe the human-companion animal relationship is doomed. I do believe it’s possible for us to have mutually beneficial symbioses.

Freddie’s story contains examples of some of the missteps we’ve taken, and some of the ways things can go wrong, but it also shows the rich, edifying, world-enlarging possibilities that are contained in an interspecies relationship. Counterintuitively, to imagine the life of another animal can end up making you more human, not less.
